Far from being a naive or utopian fantasy, sortition offers a proven, democratic, and empirically grounded path toward a government that is truly of, by, and for the people. By eliminating the incentives for corruption, dismantling the machinery of partisanship, and restoring political power to ordinary citizens, sortition represents the most honest and effective reform American democracy could ever undertake.

The most immediate and powerful argument for sortition lies in its capacity to eradicate political corruption — not by hoping politicians will be virtuous, but by removing the structural incentives that make corruption inevitable. Under the current electoral system, candidates must raise vast sums of money to compete, creating a direct pipeline from wealthy donors and special interests to legislative outcomes. Studies consistently show that lawmakers are far more responsive to the preferences of affluent citizens and organized lobbies than to the average voter. The legislator’s accountability shifts from pleasing patrons to serving the public good during a limited, non-renewable term. This mirrors the logic of the jury system: we trust randomly selected citizens to judge guilt or innocence precisely because they are immune to political pressure and personal ambition. Extending that principle to lawmaking is not a leap — it is a logical extension of our deepest democratic instincts.

Elections today are not primarily about policy or competence; they are tribal contests fought along ideological lines, fueled by media fragmentation, gerrymandering, and the psychology of negative partisanship — where voters choose not because they love their party, but because they fear the other. This dynamic rewards extremism, discourages compromise, and turns governance into a zero-sum war. Sortition disrupts this cycle by ensuring that legislative bodies reflect the actual demographic, ideological, and socioeconomic diversity of the population. A randomly selected citizen legislature would include not just activists and ideologues, but also nurses, teachers, factory workers, retirees, and small business owners — people whose lived experiences resist simplistic partisan labels. Deliberative democracy experiments, such as the Irish Citizens’ Assembly on abortion and climate change, and the Oregon Citizens’ Initiative Review, have repeatedly shown that when ordinary people are given time, information, and space to deliberate, they reach thoughtful, compromise-oriented conclusions that often elude polarized legislatures. Sortition would institutionalize this wisdom, replacing partisan combat with collaborative problem-solving grounded in shared humanity.

No one expects a randomly selected juror to be a legal expert before service — yet we trust juries to render just verdicts after deliberation and guidance. History and contemporary practice affirm that ordinary people, when equipped with support and time, are capable of sound judgment on complex issues. The ancient Athenians used sortition to fill most of their governmental offices, and modern experiments — from participatory budgeting in Porto Alegre to citizens’ assemblies in France, Canada, and the UK — demonstrate that randomly selected bodies can produce legitimate, innovative, and widely accepted outcomes. Moreover, sortition need not be applied blindly to executive roles; a hybrid model could use sortition for legislatures while retaining limited, accountable mechanisms for executive functions — though even executives could be selected from among vetted, service-oriented citizens, reducing the cult of personality that distorts presidential politics.

Most profoundly, sortition reclaims democracy from the realm of spectacle and returns it to the people. Elections, as currently conducted, are a form of political theater: billions spent on advertising, endless polling, scripted debates, and the cultivation of celebrity politicians. The United States was founded on the revolutionary idea that legitimate authority arises from the consent of the governed. In a time when faith in democracy is at historic lows, sortition is not a step into the unknown — it is a step back toward what democracy was always meant to be. Below is a detailed explanation of the supposed benefits and rationales for adopting such a system, with emphasis on how it might improve government fairness, reduce elite influence, and enhance democratic representation.

1. Improved Government Fairness: Eliminating Structural Biases in Selection

The Problem with Elections: Elections tend to favor individuals with:

  • Access to wealth (for campaign financing),
  • Name recognition (often from prior office or media exposure),
  • Social capital (networks of influence),
  • Time and flexibility to campaign (disproportionately disadvantaging working-class, caregiving, or marginalized groups),
  • Skill in performance and rhetoric (not necessarily correlated with governance competence or public-spiritedness).

This creates a selection bias that systematically excludes ordinary citizens — especially those without privileged backgrounds — from holding office.

How Sortition Improves Fairness:

  • Equal Opportunity by Design: Every adult citizen (or a defined eligible pool) has an equal statistical chance of being selected, regardless of income, education, race, gender, or social connections.
  • Descriptive Representation: A randomly selected body statistically mirrors the demographic, socioeconomic, and ideological diversity of the population. For example, if 40% of citizens are low-income, ~40% of the selected legislature would be low-income — something rarely achieved in elected bodies.
  • Procedural Justice: Selection by lottery is perceived as impartial and unbiased — unlike elections, which can be manipulated by gerrymandering, voter suppression, dark money, or media bias.

> Example: A citizens’ assembly selected by sortition in Ireland (2016–2018) successfully recommended same-sex marriage and abortion law reforms — positions that had stalled for years in the elected parliament due to partisan and religious elite resistance.

2. Reducing Elite Influence: Breaking the Cycle of Political Capture

The Problem with Elections: Elections are vulnerable to elite capture — where wealthy individuals, corporations, lobbyists, and special interest groups exert disproportionate influence through:

  • Campaign donations (often legalized bribery),
  • Revolving doors between government and industry,
  • Think tanks and media ownership shaping public discourse,
  • Incumbent advantages and party machines.

Even well-intentioned officials often become beholden to donors or party elites to survive re-election cycles.

How Sortition Reduces Elite Influence:

  • No Campaigning Needed: Since officeholders are selected by lottery, there is no need to raise money, court donors, or pledge loyalty to parties or special interests to gain office.
  • Short, Non-Renewable Terms: Most sortition proposals call for single, limited terms (e.g., 1–2 years), reducing incentives for long-term careerism and corruption.
  • Independence from Party Machines: Selected citizens are not beholden to party platforms or patronage networks; they are free to deliberate based on evidence and conscience.
  • Resistance to Lobbying: A legislature of ordinary citizens, serving temporarily and returning to civilian life, is less attractive as a target for sustained lobbying — there’s no long-term payoff for influencing them.

> Evidence: Studies of citizens’ assemblies (e.g., in Canada, France, Belgium) show participants are highly resistant to lobbying attempts and often express skepticism toward “experts” who appear to have hidden agendas.

3. Enhancing Democratic Representation: Beyond Majoritarianism to Deliberative Inclusivity

The Problem with Elections: Elections often produce:

  • Majoritarian tyranny: 51% can impose policies on 49% without meaningful deliberation.
  • Polarization: Incentivizes adversarial, zero-sum rhetoric over compromise.
  • Low civic engagement: Many citizens feel alienated, believing their vote doesn’t matter or that politicians don’t represent them.
  • Descriptive mismatch: Legislatures are overwhelmingly wealthy, male, older, and less racially diverse than the populations they serve.

How Sortition Enhances Representation:

  • Descriptive + Representation: Sortition ensures the legislature looks like the people — not just in vote share, but in lived experience (e.g., nurses, teachers, factory workers, single parents, immigrants, people with disabilities).
  • Deliberative Quality: When ordinary citizens are given time, resources, and expert facilitation to deliberate on complex issues (as in citizens’ assemblies), they produce thoughtful, nuanced, and often surprisingly consensus-driven outcomes — outperforming elected bodies in areas like climate policy, electoral reform, and end-of-life care.
  • Legitimacy Through Inclusion: When people see others “like them” making decisions, trust in government increases. This counters the perception of politics as a rigged game for elites.
  • Civic Education & Engagement: Serving in a sortition body becomes a powerful civic education experience — participants report increased political efficacy, knowledge, and willingness to engage in democracy afterward.

> Example: The French Citizens’ Convention on Climate (2019–2020), composed of 150 randomly selected citizens, proposed 149 measures to cut emissions — including banning domestic flights where train alternatives exist — many of which were adopted or influenced national policy, despite initial skepticism from politicians.

Additional Benefits Often Cited

  • Reduction in Negative Campaigning: No need for attack ads, smear campaigns, or personality-driven politics.
  • Mitigation of Gerrymandering: Since selection is random and nationwide (or stratified by region/district), geographic manipulation becomes irrelevant.
  • Encouragement of Long-Term Thinking: Without re-election pressures, sortition bodies may prioritize intergenerational justice (e.g., climate, debt, infrastructure) over short-term populist wins.
  • Diminished Role of Parties: While parties could still exist to organize policy proposals, their gatekeeping power over who governs is broken.
  • Scalability: Sortition can be applied at multiple levels — local, regional, national — and combined with elected bodies (e.g., a hybrid legislature where one chamber is elected, the other sorted).

Challenges and Criticisms (For Balance)

While the benefits are compelling, sortition is not a panacea. Critics raise valid concerns:

  • Competence: Are ordinary citizens capable of governing complex modern states? (Proponents argue: with expert briefings, facilitation, and time, yes — and often better than ideologically driven politicians.)
  • Accountability: How do you remove a poorly performing sortition official? (Solutions: recall mechanisms, post-service review, or hybrid systems where sortition bodies recommend, and elected bodies ratify.)
  • Legitimacy Perception: Some may view lottery selection as “arbitrary” or undemocratic — though surveys show high public support once the concept is explained.
  • Transition Risk: Moving from elections to sortition requires constitutional change, public education, and institutional safeguards.

Conclusion: Sortition as a Democratic Renewal Tool

A nationwide system of sortition does not necessarily seek to abolish elections entirely — many advocates propose hybrid models (e.g., a sorted upper house or citizens’ assembly that reviews or initiates legislation, while an elected lower house handles day-to-day governance). Its core promise lies in democratizing power by:

  • ✅ Making government statistically representative of the people,
  • ✅ Removing the corrupting influence of money and elite networks,
  • ✅ Fostering deliberation over polarization,
  • ✅ Restoring trust through inclusion and procedural fairness.

In an era of declining trust in institutions, rising inequality, and democratic backsliding, sortition offers a radical but empirically grounded path to renew democracy — not by changing who votes, but by changing who gets to govern. It is not a utopian fantasy, but a pragmatic experiment already working in microcosms around the world — waiting to be scaled.

> As political scientist Hélène Landemore argues: “Democracy is not about choosing the best rulers; it’s about ensuring that the rulers are a microcosm of the ruled.”
> Sortition makes that ideal a procedural reality.

Look around you. Look at the billion-dollar circuses we call campaigns, where candidates spend two years begging oligarchs for cash while ignoring our crumbling schools. Look at the gerrymandered districts that make most races about which party can better manipulate maps, not which candidate can better serve people. Look at the 40% of us who don't even bother voting anymore—because we know, deep in our bones, that the game is rigged. That "representative democracy" has become a cruel joke where the only things being represented are special interests and naked ambition.

The problem isn't who's winning our elections. The problem is elections themselves.

We have created a system that selects for the exact opposite of what a republic needs. It rewards the loudest, not the wisest. The most photogenic, not the most principled. The best fundraisers, not the best listeners. We have replaced the wisdom of crowds with the tyranny of charisma, and we wonder why our leaders fail us.

But what if there was another way? A way to guarantee true representation. A way to make corruption nearly impossible. A way to ensure that power flows not to those who crave it most, but to those who deserve it least—precisely because they never sought it at all.

I am talking about sortition: the random selection of our leaders by lottery.

Imagine it. Imagine a House of Representatives where any of the 330 million Americans could be called to serve—teachers and truck drivers, nurses and construction workers, grandmothers and students. No campaigns. No fundraising. No corporate PACs. No gerrymandering. No party bosses deciding who gets to run. Just pure, mathematical fairness: every citizen an equal chance to govern.

This is not madness. This is democracy in its purest form—the democracy of Athens, where the lottery was considered more democratic than elections because it couldn't be captured by elites. The democracy of our own jury system, where we trust random selection to decide life-and-death decisions because we know it's less corruptible than any other method.

Anti-corruption? Try bribing a legislature when you don't know who will be in it next year. Try buying an election when there is no election. The entire architecture of corruption—donors, lobbyists, Super PACs, revolving doors—comes crashing down when leadership is temporary, random, and cannot be self-perpetuating. A randomly selected citizen-legislator doesn't need to worry about being re-elected; they only need to worry about doing right by their conscience and their country.

Empowerment? For the first time, every single American would have an equal claim to power. Not the illusion of power through a vote that gets drowned in a sea of money, but actual, tangible power to sit in the room where decisions are made. Think of what that does to the psychology of citizenship. When you know you could be called to serve, you pay attention. You learn. You engage. Maybe it's time to remember that the Constitution was written by farmers and merchants, not career politicians.

This is not a call for anarchy. This is a call for the deepest structural reform since the abolition of the monarchy. We would keep our Constitution, our rights, our courts. We would simply replace the corruptible middlemen of elections with the incorruptible mathematics of randomness.

The Founders feared the tyranny of the majority. But they never imagined the tyranny of the donor class. They feared mob rule, but they never dreamed of a system where 0.01% of the population could bankroll an entire election cycle.

We have tried elections. For 250 years, we have tried them. And they have failed us. They have delivered us into the hands of an aristocracy more entrenched than anything the Founders rebelled against—an aristocracy of campaign donors, media conglomerates, and professional political dynasties.

The time for tinkering is over. We cannot reform this system. We must replace it.

I say to you today: let us be the generation that finally makes good on the promise of "We the People." Let us tear down the temples of electoral idolatry and replace them with a simple, sacred lottery drum. Let us trust ourselves—ordinary, imperfect, glorious Americans—to govern ourselves.

Give me random selection over manufactured consent. Give me sortition over sedition. Give me a citizen's humility over a politician's ambition.

Let us abolish elections—not to end democracy, but to finally begin it.

The power is ours. We only need the courage to randomize it.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of replacing all elections in the United States with a system of sortition, where legislative and executive leaders are chosen through random citizen selection, emphasizing how this approach removes political corruption, reduces partisanship, and empowers ordinary people.
Model Response:

In an era of deep polarization, record campaign spending, and a pervasive sense that government serves the wealthy and well‑connected over ordinary citizens, the United States faces a crisis of democratic legitimacy. Many blame apathy, misinformation, or “bad politicians.” But there is a more fundamental problem: the electoral system itself. When political power is awarded through expensive, competitive campaigns, it inevitably becomes entangled with money, marketing, manipulation, and permanent partisanship.

There is a radically different model, one with deep historical roots and growing contemporary support: sortition, or the random selection of citizens for public office. Instead of voting for candidates in elections, legislative and executive leaders would be chosen the way we choose jurors: from the citizenry at large, by lottery, with fair procedures and clear eligibility rules.

Replacing elections with a system of sortition would transform American governance. It would sharply reduce political corruption, weaken the grip of parties and factions, and empower ordinary people to shape the laws that govern their lives. Far from being a utopian fantasy, sortition is a practical, proven method of decision-making that we already trust with matters of life and death in jury trials. Extending it to political leadership would bring government closer to the democratic ideal it claims to embody.

What Sortition Is—and Why It’s More Democratic Than Elections

Sortition is the random selection of decision-makers from a defined group—in this case, the adult citizen population. The basic idea is simple:

  • Define who is eligible (e.g., citizens over 18 without disqualifying conflicts, with basic civic competence).
  • Randomly select a representative sample, stratified by factors like region, age, and perhaps income, to mirror the population.
  • Give those citizens real power, time, staff support, and access to information.
  • Rotate them regularly, with fixed terms and no immediate re-selection.

This is not an untested theory. Ancient Athens, often regarded as the birthplace of democracy, used sortition for most public offices. They saw elections as aristocratic—favoring the wealthy, eloquent, and well-known—while lotteries gave each citizen an equal chance to rule and be ruled in turn. Today, many countries use citizen assemblies chosen by lottery to deliberate on issues like climate policy, constitutional reforms, and electoral rules. These bodies consistently show that ordinary people, given the right conditions, can make thoughtful, informed decisions.

If democracy means rule by the people, not rule by those able to fund, win, and survive election campaigns, then sortition is more democratic than elections, not less.

1. Removing Political Corruption at the Root

Corruption is not just about criminals stuffing envelopes with cash. It is also about the subtle, legalized ways in which power and money intertwine: campaign contributions that shape policy, lobbying that rewrites laws, and the revolving door between government and industry. Elections create a structural dependence of politicians on donors, parties, and interest groups. Sortition breaks that dependence by removing the need to win elections.

No Campaigns, No Campaign Money

In an electoral system, anyone seeking office must:

  • Raise large sums of money.
  • Build name recognition through advertising and media.
  • Secure support from parties, donors, and networks.

Each of these steps creates obligations—to sponsors, party leaders, ideological blocs—that can conflict with the public interest. Even honest politicians must constantly think about reelection: “How will this vote play with donors? Will this decision anger my base?”

Under sortition:

  • There are no campaigns. No one runs, advertises, or fundraises.
  • Citizens are chosen by lottery, with no financial barrier to entry.
  • No candidate can “buy” influence or manipulate voters to gain office.

This single change would instantly eliminate the entire industry of campaign finance: the super PACs, the dark money groups, and the permanent fundraising apparatus that distorts policy. It removes the incentive for wealthy individuals and corporations to invest in “buying access” because there is nobody to sponsor and no campaign to finance.

No Career Politicians, No Permanent Political Class

Elections produce a professional political class: people who make a career out of winning office, staying in office, and then cashing out through lobbying or corporate roles. They accumulate connections and cultivate donors over decades, becoming more beholden to political survival than to independent judgment.

With sortition:

  • Terms would be limited and non-renewable (or not renewable for a long period).
  • Officeholders return to ordinary life after their term.
  • There is no path to a long-term political career dependent on cultivating powerful patrons.

Because randomly selected citizens cannot campaign to stay in office, they are free to make unpopular but necessary decisions. They would be more likely to ask: “What is right and beneficial long-term?” instead of “What will help me win the next election?”

Lobbying Loses Its Grip

In the current system, interest groups target legislators and executives who:

  • Depend on donations.
  • Have stable positions for many years.
  • Plan to remain in political networks after office.

A rotating, randomly selected citizen body is much harder to capture:

  • Members only serve for a relatively short stint, then leave.
  • They are not entrenched in political professional networks.
  • They do not need future campaign funding or party support.

Lobbying does not disappear—but it must become informational rather than transactional. Groups can still present arguments and evidence, but the classic tools of influence—donations, promises of endorsements, future jobs—lose their power.

2. Reducing Partisanship and Polarization

American politics is trapped in partisan warfare. Elections incentivize parties to treat politics as a zero-sum game where victory matters more than governance. Every issue becomes a symbolic battlefield for mobilizing the base, not a problem to be pragmatically solved. Sortition changes that dynamic at a structural level.

No Electoral Incentive to Polarize

Parties thrive by mobilizing loyal voters and demonizing opponents. It is often easier to win by stoking fear and outrage than by solving complex problems. Politicians gain attention by being extreme; they lose donations and media oxygen by being moderate and cooperative.

Randomly chosen citizens have no need to excite a base or perform for cameras:

  • They do not stand for reelection.
  • They do not need party endorsements or ideological purity credentials.
  • They are not rewarded for grandstanding; they are judged only by the quality of their decisions.

As a result, incentives shift from “defeat the other side” to “figure out what actually works.” People chosen by sortition can compromise without being accused of betrayal; they can listen to evidence that contradicts prior beliefs without fearing primary challengers.

Real Deliberation Instead of Permanent Campaign

Election-centered politics pushes debate into sound bites and slogans. Legislative bodies often perform more for TV clips than for policy outcomes. Citizens, seeing these performances, conclude that politics is a spectacle rather than a serious public endeavor.

Sortition-based bodies can be designed to foster genuine deliberation:

  • Structured hearings and testimony from competing experts.
  • Smaller committees for deep study, feeding into larger assemblies.
  • Time and training dedicated to understanding complex issues.

Randomly selected citizens typically behave differently than professional politicians. Citizens’ assemblies around the world show consistent patterns: people listen more, revise their positions, and seek common ground when they are not under the pressure of party discipline or electoral performance.

Ordinary Diversity, Not Ideological Extremes

Elections often yield representatives who are more ideologically extreme than the average voter. Primaries amplify the voice of highly engaged, partisan activists, while moderate or disengaged citizens stay home.

Sortition, by its nature, gives you a cross-section of society:

  • Parents, workers, retirees, students.
  • People with different incomes, backgrounds, and experiences.
  • Those who would never dream of running for office but have valuable perspectives.

This diversity tempers ideological extremes. A randomly selected assembly is more likely to reflect the broad, pragmatic middle of society—people who care about practical outcomes in healthcare, education, safety, and economic stability—rather than the fringes that dominate primary elections and partisan media.

3. Empowering Ordinary People and Restoring Legitimacy

Many Americans feel politically powerless. They vote, if at all, for candidates they barely know, constrained by a narrow menu offered by parties and donors. Once elected, officials often seem distant, unresponsive, and insulated from ordinary concerns. Sortition directly empowers citizens by inviting them into the core of decision-making.

Real Representation, Not Symbolic

In an electoral system, representation is indirect and often distorted:

  • A handful of representatives speak for hundreds of thousands of constituents each.
  • Safe districts and partisan gerrymandering further skew who gets “represented.”
  • Many groups—especially the poor, minorities, and young people—are chronically underrepresented among officeholders.

Sortition makes representation literal:

  • The legislature is composed of ordinary citizens statistically matched to the population.
  • Inequalities in money and media influence do not affect who gets selected.
  • The lived experience of most social groups is present in the room, not filtered through a professional political lens.

When people see bodies of government that actually look like them—people of different backgrounds, not just wealthy professionals—they are more likely to see decisions as legitimate, even when they disagree with specific outcomes.

Civic Growth Through Service

Serving in office under sortition could be treated as a civic duty, like jury duty but with more time, support, and recognition. Rather than politics being a distant, specialized profession, governance becomes a shared responsibility.

Such service can:

  • Develop citizens’ political understanding and skills.
  • Spread civic knowledge more evenly through society.
  • Build empathy across social lines as people with different backgrounds collaborate.

Over time, thousands or millions of citizens would have direct experience in governing institutions, creating a more politically educated public. Political engagement becomes experiential and practical, not just ideological or symbolic.

Breaking the Cynical Cycle

Currently, many Americans see politics as rigged, corrupt, or pointless. Turnout is low. Distrust is high. This cynicism becomes self-reinforcing: people withdraw, leaving more power in the hands of organized and wealthy minorities.

Sortition offers a dramatic break from this pattern. By visibly dismantling the machinery of campaign cash and party manipulation, it signals that government is truly being shared:

  • No one can argue they “never had a chance” because everyone literally has a chance to serve.
  • Decisions are made in public by ordinary people, not behind closed doors by professionals beholden to donors.
  • The emphasis shifts from choosing rulers to actively participating in rule.

When a policy emerges from months of work by a representative sample of ordinary citizens, it carries a different moral weight than when it emerges from partisan bargaining and lobbying.

Addressing Common Objections

Objection 1: “Random citizens aren’t competent to govern.”

We already trust random citizens with enormous responsibilities: jury duty. Jurors, chosen by lot, decide on guilt or innocence in criminal cases and award damages in complex civil disputes. They make these decisions after hearing evidence, receiving instructions, and deliberating—exactly the kind of support that sortition-based political bodies would have.

Governance under sortition would include:

  • Robust training on the issues and procedures.
  • Access to independent experts and nonpartisan staff.
  • Division into committees so people can specialize.

Competence does not require career politicians; it requires good information, time, and collective deliberation. Ordinary citizens live with the consequences of policy every day—they have strong incentives to get it right.

Objection 2: “Random selection could empower extremists or the ignorant.”

In any large population, there are some extremists and some poorly informed individuals. But sortition works with groups, not individuals. A large body chosen randomly will statistically mirror the population. Extremists will be rare and isolated; they won’t dominate the discussion.

Moreover:

  • Deliberation tends to moderate extreme positions.
  • Exposure to diverse views and evidence reduces ignorance.
  • Structured procedures can prevent a few individuals from hijacking the process.

Elections, by contrast, often reward those who appeal most successfully to fear, anger, or narrow interests. The evidence from citizens’ assemblies shows that ordinary citizens, when empowered and informed, tend to become more thoughtful and moderate, not more extreme.

Objection 3: “We need accountability, and elections are how we hold leaders accountable.”

Elections provide a kind of accountability—but a very blunt and often ineffective one. Voters must judge leaders on long lists of issues, past promises, and media narratives, with rarely any clear, direct link between their vote and specific decisions.

Sortition allows for different, more precise forms of accountability:

  • Clear term limits and rotation ensure no one holds power too long.
  • Open procedures, recorded debates, and transparency let the public see who argued for what.
  • Independent oversight bodies (also chosen by sortition or mixed methods) can review for corruption, conflicts of interest, and abuses.

Accountability is not synonymous with elections. Courts, audits, public reporting, and transparent processes can provide more meaningful oversight than the occasional, highly mediated choice between two professional politicians.

A Path Forward: From Thought Experiment to Reform

Transitioning from elections to sortition would be a profound change that must happen legally and peacefully, through constitutional reform and broad public consent. It need not be instantaneous or total. A sensible path might include:

  • Introducing sortition-based citizens’ assemblies with advisory powers on major issues.
  • Gradually shifting parts of legislative power—like redistricting, ethics oversight, or budget review—to randomly selected bodies.
  • Using successful experiments to build public trust and familiarity.
  • Ultimately reforming constitutional structures, through democratic procedures, to institutionalize sortition for legislative and executive roles.

Each stage can be evaluated based on outcomes: Are decisions better informed? Is public trust rising? Is corruption decreasing? Are policies more stable and broadly acceptable?

The point is not to impose an untested fantasy, but to evolve toward a system that better embodies the core promise of democracy: that power rests with the people, not with a self-perpetuating political class.

Conclusion: Completing the Democratic Revolution

The United States rightly celebrates its democratic heritage, yet its politics are dominated by money, entrenched parties, and a narrow professional elite. Elections, once heralded as the signature institution of democracy, have become a bottleneck through which all power must pass—corrupted by wealth, poisoned by partisanship, and increasingly detached from the daily realities of ordinary citizens.

Sortition offers a way to complete the democratic revolution, not abandon it. By replacing elections with random selection:

  • Corruption is cut off at its source, as the competition for office—and with it the need for donors and sponsors—disappears.
  • Partisanship loses its structural advantages, replaced by genuine deliberation among diverse citizens.
  • Ordinary people are not merely voters, but direct participants in governance, sharing the burdens and responsibilities of public decision-making.

We already accept that ordinary citizens, chosen by lot, can judge evidence and make life-altering decisions in a courtroom. There is no principled reason to deny them the same trust in a legislature or executive council designed for sortition. The question is not whether citizens are “good enough” to govern, but whether we are willing to build institutions that treat them as such.

Replacing elections with sortition is a bold proposal, but boldness is precisely what a failing system requires. If we truly believe in government of the people, by the people, and for the people, we should take seriously the one mechanism that gives every person an equal chance to wield power: the humble, revolutionary lottery.

Sortition systems therefore could be:

  • Better at addressing problems that elections encourage politicians to delay or minimize.

8. Civic culture and sense of shared responsibility

8.1 Turning politics into a civic duty, not a spectator sport

  • Jury duty already:

    • Symbolizes shared responsibility for justice.
    • Tells citizens, “You might be called; your judgment matters.”

  • Sortition extends this to governance:

    • People know they or their neighbors might be called to serve.
    • Politics becomes something ordinary people do, not just pundits and professionals.

This can:

  • Increase political literacy (people learn more knowing they might serve).
  • Enhance trust (you’re more likely to trust decisions made by a body that could have included you).

8.2 Reducing alienation and “anti‑politics” sentiment

  • Many people see politicians as a separate, self‑serving class.
  • Sortition counteracts that by literally making politicians “just people”:
    • Teachers, plumbers, parents, retirees, students.
    • People who share the everyday concerns of the public.

This can:

  • Decrease cynicism.
  • Make government feel more like “us” and less like “them.”

9. Potential roles for sortition in a national system

Even if one doesn’t replace elections entirely, nationwide sortition can be adopted in ways that capture many of the benefits:

  • A second (or first) national legislative chamber chosen entirely by lot.
  • Randomly selected:
    • Ethics councils overseeing corruption and conflicts of interest.
    • Appointment commissions for judges, regulators, or public broadcasters.
    • Constitutional and major‑reform conventions, whose proposals go to referendum.

Each of these:

  • Dilutes elite capture.
  • Inserts representative, deliberative bodies that “speak for the public” without needing to win elections.

10. Summary of main benefits

A nationwide system of sortition, if carefully designed, can:

  • Improve fairness

    • Equalize the opportunity to hold power.
    • Reduce structural advantages of wealth, status, and insider connections.
    • Bring marginalized perspectives directly into decision‑making.

  • Reduce elite influence

    • Remove campaign finance as the main route to power.
    • Weaken the lobbyist–politician–donor triangle.
    • Disrupt political dynasties and party control over candidate selection.

  • Enhance democratic representation

    • Produce legislatures that look more like the population.
    • Harness cognitive and life‑experience diversity for better decisions.
    • Move politics from permanent campaigning to informed, long‑term deliberation by ordinary citizens.

There are serious design questions and challenges, but these are the core reasons supporters see sortition as a powerful way to make government fairer, less captured by elites, and more genuinely representative of the people.

The kind where everyone genuinely gets an equal shot at power.

My fellow Americans,

We are told, from the day we learn the Pledge of Allegiance, that we live in a government “of the people, by the people, for the people.”

But look around you.

Does our government feel “of” us, when nearly every serious candidate must be a millionaire or backed by millionaires?

Does it feel “by” us, when 90% of congressional races are decided before a single ballot is cast, locked in by gerrymandered maps and party machines?

Does it feel “for” us, when the policies that pass are the policies favored by donors and lobbyists—not by the majority of citizens?

We cling to the ritual of elections as if they are sacred, as if they are the only possible expression of democracy. But elections, as we practice them, have become a marketplace where power is bought and sold. The price is paid in dollars—and the cost is paid by every ordinary person who is shut out.

It is time to confront a heresy in American political religion: elections, as our primary method of choosing leaders, are failing us. And there is a better way.

That alternative is called sortition: the random selection of ordinary citizens—like jury duty—to serve as our lawmakers and executives.

Tonight, I stand before you not to tear down democracy, but to complete it. Not to abandon self-government, but to reclaim it from the grip of money, manipulation, and permanent political class.

I am asking you to imagine a United States where the halls of power look like us, live like us, and answer to us—because they are us.

Elections: A Noble Idea, Corrupted in Practice

Elections sound fair in theory. You vote, your neighbor votes, and the person with the most support wins. Simple. Elegant.

But in the real world, that’s not what happens.

In the real world, elections select for three traits above all others:

  • Ability to raise massive sums of money
  • Ability to market and brand yourself like a product
  • Ability to survive, and thrive, inside a permanent campaign

These are not the same traits as wisdom, integrity, or good judgment.

We have built a system where:

  • Candidates spend more time fundraising than legislating.
  • Lobbyists draft laws that elected officials barely read.
  • Parties and consultants fine-tune every word we hear, not to tell the truth, but to win the next news cycle.

Is it any wonder that trust in government is at historic lows?
Is it any wonder that people don’t vote, not out of apathy, but out of disgust?

We were promised rule by the people. We got rule by professionals—political professionals, donor professionals, influence professionals. A permanent political class that cycles between elected office, lobbying firms, think tanks, and media appearances. Elections have become their job security, not our safeguard.

If we keep doing what we have always done, we will keep getting what we have always got:

  • Polarization instead of problem-solving
  • Soundbites instead of substance
  • Gridlock instead of governance

We don’t need a new slogan, or a new party, or a new campaign finance rule. We need a new way to choose our leaders.

Sortition: Democracy Without the Price Tag

Sortition is ancient and yet radical: instead of electing leaders through expensive, corruptible campaigns, we randomly select citizens to serve, for limited terms, with proper support and training.

You already trust this system with something incredibly serious: your life and liberty.

We use sortition for juries.

We don’t elect jurors. We don’t ask them to raise money or run ads. We don’t hold debates between “pro-conviction” and “pro-acquittal” candidates. We randomly summon ordinary citizens, vet them for basic conflicts of interest, and then ask them to make life-and-death decisions.

Why? Because we recognize something profound:
A group of diverse, ordinary people, given time, information, and a clear responsibility, can weigh evidence more fairly than a single powerful judge—or a political appointee beholden to donors.

Now imagine if we applied that same trust, that same faith in each other, to lawmaking.

Imagine a Congress where:

  • Members are selected like jurors from the entire adult population.
  • Rich and poor, rural and urban, Democrat and Republican and independent—all thrown together by chance.
  • They serve one term, then go back to their lives. No re-election campaigns. No donors to please. No war chests to build.

Imagine executives—governors, even a president—selected from panels of citizens chosen by lot, screened only for basic competence and integrity, then supported by professional civil servants and expert advisors.

This is not fantasy. Versions of this system have worked:

  • In ancient Athens, sortition was central to democracy. Most offices were filled by lot because elections were seen as aristocratic and corruptible.
  • Today, citizens’ assemblies selected by lot in Ireland, Canada, France, and other countries have helped resolve deeply divisive issues with more wisdom and less rage than elected bodies.

We trust randomness to be fair in lotteries, in juries, in scientific experiments. Why not in democracy?

Fairness: One Person, One Real Chance

Elections promise “one person, one vote.”
Sortition offers something more: one person, one real chance.

Right now, your “chance” of holding office is effectively zero unless:

  • You have wealth or access to those who do.
  • You are willing to live in a permanent spotlight.
  • You are ready to bend, compromise, and deal just to survive in a brutal electoral arena.

Under sortition:

  • Every adult citizen has an equal statistical chance of being called to serve.
  • No one can buy better odds. No super PAC can tilt the process.
  • Representation stops being symbolic and becomes literal.

Think about what “representation” actually means. Today, Congress “represents” teachers and truckers, nurses and small business owners, single parents and retirees—but almost none of those people ever actually sit in Congress.

In a sortition-based legislature, teachers and truckers, nurses and small business owners, single parents and retirees are the legislature.

Fairness is not having a millionaire say they “understand” your struggle.
Fairness is having people who live your struggle at the table of power.

Anti-Corruption: You Can’t Bribe a Lottery

Corruption feeds on dependency. Elected officials are dependent on:

  • Big donors for campaign funds.
  • Parties for endorsements and infrastructure.
  • Lobbyists for information and post-office careers.

Even the most honest representatives are trapped in a system that pressures them to think: “How will this affect my re-election?” every time they vote.

When leaders are selected by sortition:

  • There are no campaigns to finance. No TV ads to buy. No war chests to fill.
  • You can’t predict who will be in office next, so you can’t invest in them years ahead.
  • You can’t pressure a citizen representative with the threat of funding their opponent—because they have no opponent.

The incentive flips. Instead of serving donors to stay in power, citizens serve the public because they only have power once, for a limited time, under intense transparency.

Imagine:

  • Strict rules against lobbying citizen-legislators during their term.
  • Full disclosure of meetings and communications.
  • Severe penalties for bribery, with no “campaign contribution” fig leaf.

When power rotates like a jury pool instead of calcifying into a political class, corruption has nowhere to sink its roots.

Empowering Ordinary Citizens: From Audience to Authors

Right now, politics trains us to be spectators. We watch candidates. We watch debates. We watch scandals unfold. Our job is to cheer or boo every two or four years, then go home.

Sortition says: you are not just an audience. You are a potential author of our collective future.

Imagine getting a letter in the mail:

> “You have been selected to serve in the National Citizens’ Assembly for a term of two years. You will receive a salary, child care support, training, and the respect owed to a public servant. Your duty is to deliberate and legislate on behalf of your fellow citizens.”

Maybe you’re a mechanic. A cashier. A nurse. A programmer. A farmer. Maybe you’ve never given a political speech in your life.

But you know what rent costs.
You know what health care costs.
You know what a broken school or a broken bridge looks like.
You know what it feels like to be ignored by people in power.

Sortition says: that lived experience is not a side note to democracy. It is the raw material of democratic wisdom.

We know this already from citizens’ juries and assemblies:
When ordinary people are given time, information, and a real responsibility, they rise to it. They ask hard questions. They listen. They revise their opinions. They weigh trade-offs. They compromise without selling out.

Our current system treats us as consumers of politics.
Sortition treats us as producers of politics.

“But Won’t We Get Incompetent Leaders?”

We must face the obvious question:
“Isn’t this risky? Won’t random selection give us unqualified people?”

I ask you: compared to what?

Right now, we already have leaders who:

  • Ignore basic facts and science.
  • Confuse showmanship with leadership.
  • Use office as a stepping stone to media careers and private wealth.

Elections haven’t filtered out incompetence; they’ve invited in a specific kind of performative incompetence.

Under sortition:

  • We can set baseline requirements: age, basic education or literacy, absence of serious criminal convictions, mental competence. The pool is still huge.
  • We can provide training: crash courses in law, economics, ethics, and the specific policy issues on the agenda. Just as we train jurors, we can train citizen-legislators.
  • We can surround them with a professional, non-partisan civil service for technical expertise—while the citizens make the value judgments.

And remember: the power of sortition is collective intelligence. We aren’t putting one random person on a throne. We are gathering hundreds of randomly selected people and asking them to deliberate, to learn from experts and from each other.

If we trust twelve strangers in a jury box to understand evidence and decide guilt or innocence, why can’t we trust five hundred strangers to understand testimony and decide public policy?

Competence isn’t born in campaigns. It is built through responsibility.

A Peaceful, Practical Path Forward

I am not calling for chaos. I am not calling for revolution in the streets. The path to sortition can be legal, gradual, and tested step by step.

We can start small:

  • Citizens’ assemblies by sortition to advise on complex policy issues at local and state levels.
  • Mixed bodies where some legislators are elected and some are chosen by lot, allowing us to compare performance.
  • Randomly selected oversight boards for policing, environmental regulation, and public ethics.

We can build trust. We can gather data. We can refine the process.

Over time, as people see the difference—see ordinary citizens doing serious, honest work while elected bodies grandstand and stall—support for deeper reform will grow.

Constitutional change is possible. The Constitution has been amended many times. Slavery was ended. Women gained the right to vote. Senators shifted from being appointed by state legislatures to being directly elected. Our structure is not sacred stone; it is a living design.

We can amend it again to reflect a deeper understanding of democracy: that the fairest way to share power is not to sell it to the highest bidder every few years, but to rotate it among us all.

The Courage to Trust Each Other

At the heart of this proposal is not a technical argument. It is a moral one.

Do we trust each other?

Elections tell a story:
“Some of us are leaders, and most of us are followers. The leaders are the ones who can afford to run, who can flatter our hopes and stoke our fears, who can dominate the conversation. Put them on a stage. Let them battle. Choose your champion and hope they remember you.”

Sortition tells a different story:
“Any of us can lead, because leadership is service, not celebrity. We will share that service. We will take turns. We will help each other. We will not worship candidates. We will empower citizens.”

To abolish elections as our main way of choosing leaders is not to abandon democracy. It is to say that democracy is too important to be left to campaigns.

Democracy is a promise we make to each other:

  • That no one is permanently above or below.
  • That power will not harden into a caste.
  • That every voice does not merely count at the ballot box—but may, at any time, be called to sit at the table of power.

My fellow Americans, it is time to be as bold as the generations who came before us. They broke with kings. They broke with slavery. They expanded the circle of those who could vote. Now we must expand the circle of those who can govern.

Let us imagine a United States where Congress is not a distant theater, but a rotating cross-section of our own communities. Where decision-makers are neighbors, not brands. Where the question we ask is no longer, “Who will we vote for?” but “When will I be ready to serve?”

Let us have the courage to trust ourselves—and each other.

Let us retire elections from their throne and invite sortition to take its place, not as a trick or a shortcut, but as a deeper realization of what democracy truly means:
Not rule by the best marketers, but rule by all of us, in turn.

Thank you.

Title: The Democratic Promise of Sortition: Replacing Elections with Random Selection to Restore Power to the People

The United States, a nation founded on the revolutionary principle that governments derive “their just powers from the consent of the governed,” now faces a crisis of legitimacy. Elections, once hailed as the cornerstone of democracy, have become dominated by money, extreme partisanship, and a ruling class that appears increasingly detached from ordinary citizens. Public trust in Congress hovers around 20%, with many Americans convinced that their elected officials prioritize corporate lobbyists and partisan agendas over the common good. It is time to consider a radical alternative: replacing elections entirely with a system of sortition—randomly selecting ordinary citizens to serve as legislators and executive leaders. While the idea may seem unorthodox, sortition offers a pathway to eradicate political corruption, dissolve partisan gridlock, and truly empower the people.

Removing Corruption at Its Source

Corruption in American politics is not merely a series of isolated scandals; it is structural. The need to raise astronomical sums for campaigns creates a dependency on wealthy donors, corporations, and special interest groups. Elected officials spend a staggering proportion of their time fundraising, and the quid pro quo of political contributions is well-documented. Studies have shown that legislative outcomes align far more closely with the preferences of major donors than with those of the general public. This system fundamentally undermines the principle of political equality.

Sortition eliminates the root cause of this corruption by removing elections altogether. When leaders are chosen by lot, there is no campaign to fund, no donors to appease, and no need to pander to powerful interests. Randomly selected citizens would serve short, fixed terms and would not be eligible for re-election, eliminating any incentive to build a war chest or cultivate special relationships. The very architecture of corruption would crumble. In its place, we would have legislators motivated solely by the public good, not by the pressures of fundraising or the promise of future lucrative lobbying gigs. The influence of money would vanish, restoring a government truly of, by, and for the people.

Dissolving Partisanship Through Deliberative Diversity

Partisanship has reached toxic levels, with Congress often paralyzed by ideological warfare. Elected officials are selected through party primaries that reward extremism and polarization; they are incentivized to prioritize party loyalty over compromise. The result is a legislative body where bipartisanship is seen as betrayal, andGridlock is the norm.

Sortition would break this cycle by assembling a representative cross-section of the populace—a body that reflects the full diversity of American society, including its political views. When people are randomly selected, they bring their genuine perspectives, not a pre-packaged party platform. Evidence from modern citizens’ assemblies, such as Ireland’s conventions on same-sex marriage and abortion, demonstrates that ordinary people, when given the time and resources to deliberate, can reach consensus on contentious issues. They listen to each other, find common ground, and prioritize practical solutions over partisan wins. A legislature chosen by sortition would naturally be more moderate, collaborative, and focused on problem-solving. Without the need to answer to a party base or to campaign contributors, representatives would be free to follow their conscience and the public interest, effectively ending the corrosive influence of hyper-partisanship.

Empowering Ordinary People

Elections are not the inclusive, meritocratic processes we imagine. They are heavily skewed toward candidates with wealth, name recognition, and established networks. Women, minorities, working-class individuals, and younger citizens are vastly underrepresented in elected office. The barriers to entry—fundraising, party endorsements, media exposure—are insurmountable for most. As a result, the legislative agenda is set by a narrow elite that often fails to grasp the lived realities of the majority.

Without party machines to dictate their votes, these citizens would be compelled to listen, debate, and find common ground. The Case for Sortition: Why Random Selection Should Replace Elections in America

Reclaiming Democracy from the Political Class

The United States faces a crisis of democratic legitimacy. Congressional approval ratings hover near historic lows, routinely dipping below 20 percent. Voter turnout remains among the lowest in the developed world. Trust in government has plummeted from over 70 percent in the 1960s to barely 20 percent today. Partisan tribalism has reached levels unseen since the Civil War, and the influence of money in politics has transformed representative government into something closer to oligarchy. Americans across the political spectrum share a gnawing sense that the system is broken — that elections no longer produce governance that serves the people.

There is a solution, one with deep roots in the very origins of democracy itself: sortition, the selection of political leaders by random lottery from the citizen population. Rather than continuing to tinker with a fundamentally compromised electoral system — adding campaign finance regulations that get circumvented, drawing districts that get gerrymandered, passing ethics rules that get ignored — the United States should replace elections entirely with a system of random citizen selection for legislative and executive leadership. This radical proposal is, in fact, a return to first principles. It would eliminate political corruption at its structural source, dissolve the hyper-partisanship that paralyzes governance, and restore genuine power to ordinary citizens. Sortition is not a utopian fantasy; it is an evidence-supported, historically grounded, and philosophically sound approach to self-governance that deserves serious consideration as the successor to a failing electoral model.

I. The Athenian Precedent: Sortition as Original Democracy

To understand sortition, one must first recognize that elections were never considered democratic by the people who invented democracy. The Athenians who created the concept in the fifth century BCE used random selection — not elections — as their primary mechanism of governance. The boule, the 500-member council that set the legislative agenda for Athens, was chosen entirely by lot. Most magistrates were selected by lot. Juries were chosen by lot. Elections were reserved for only a narrow set of positions, primarily military generals, precisely because the Athenians regarded elections as an aristocratic mechanism — a method for selecting the "best" (aristos) rather than empowering the many.

Aristotle made this distinction explicitly in his Politics: "The appointment of magistrates by lot is thought to be democratic, and the election of them oligarchical." This was not a fringe view but the consensus understanding throughout classical political thought. When the American founders chose elections as their mechanism of governance, they were consciously selecting the aristocratic model. James Madison wrote openly in Federalist No. 10 about the purpose of representation as a "refinement" that would "refine and enlarge the public views by passing them through the medium of a chosen body of citizens." The system was designed to filter out the common person and elevate a natural aristocracy of talent and, frankly, wealth.

For over two centuries, Americans have been told that elections equal democracy. But elections are merely one method of selecting leaders, and they are a method that carries enormous structural baggage — baggage that sortition entirely avoids. If we are serious about government of, by, and for the people, we should look to the mechanism that the inventors of democracy actually trusted to achieve that goal.

II. Eliminating Corruption at Its Structural Root

The most powerful argument for sortition is that it eliminates political corruption not through regulation but through structural design. Corruption in the current system is not an aberration; it is a feature. The electoral model creates a class of professional politicians who require enormous sums of money to gain and retain power. The 2020 election cycle cost over $14 billion. The average winning Senate campaign costs over $10 million. This money must come from somewhere, and it comes overwhelmingly from wealthy donors, corporations, and special interest groups who expect returns on their investment.

No amount of campaign finance reform has successfully addressed this problem. McCain-Feingold was gutted by Citizens United. Public financing systems have been overwhelmed by super PACs. Disclosure requirements are routinely circumvented through dark money networks. The problem is not insufficient regulation — the problem is that the electoral system inherently requires the exchange of money for political power. As long as candidates must raise funds to win elections, those with the most resources will exert disproportionate influence over who governs and how they govern.

Sortition eliminates this dynamic entirely. When leaders are chosen by lottery, there is no campaign to finance. There is no candidate to buy. Lobbyists cannot target their spending toward sympathetic politicians because there are no politicians seeking reelection. The revolving door between government and industry loses its hinges — a randomly selected citizen serving a single term has no reason to curry favor with future employers in the private sector, because their selection was not based on connections or ambition but on chance.

Consider the practical implications. Under sortition, a pharmaceutical company cannot spend millions supporting a senator who will then block drug pricing legislation. A fossil fuel conglomerate cannot fund the campaigns of representatives who will weaken environmental regulations. A tech giant cannot cultivate relationships with committee chairs who oversee their industry. The entire infrastructure of legalized corruption — the fundraisers, the PACs, the bundlers, the lobbying firms — becomes obsolete overnight. Not because we pass a law against it, but because the structural incentive for it no longer exists.

Critics will argue that corruption would simply take new forms — that powerful interests would bribe randomly selected citizens. But this objection actually highlights the advantage of sortition. Bribing a single legislator in a body of hundreds provides minimal leverage, especially when that legislator serves a limited term and will soon be replaced by another random citizen. The cost-benefit calculation of corruption shifts dramatically. In the current system, a corporation invests in a politician who may serve for decades and accumulate enormous committee power. Under sortition, there are no long-serving power brokers to capture. Corruption becomes far more expensive, far less reliable, and far easier to detect and prosecute.

III. Dissolving Partisanship and Tribalism

American politics has become a war between two entrenched tribes. Republicans and Democrats no longer merely disagree on policy; they view each other as existential threats to the nation. Research from the Pew Research Center shows that partisan antipathy has reached unprecedented levels, with majorities in both parties viewing the opposition not just as misguided but as a genuine danger to the country. This tribalism is not a natural outgrowth of political disagreement — it is a direct product of the electoral system.

Elections incentivize division. Candidates win by mobilizing their base and demonizing the opposition. Political parties function as brands, and brand loyalty is maintained through fear and outrage. The primary system rewards extremism, pushing candidates toward the poles of their parties to survive intraparty challenges, then forcing awkward pivots toward the center for general elections. The result is a political class that is systematically more extreme, more combative, and more performative than the population it claims to represent.

Sortition dissolves this dynamic because it eliminates the conditions that create it. A randomly selected legislature would have no parties, no caucuses built around electoral survival, no leadership structures designed to enforce party discipline. Citizens chosen by lot would come to governance with their own views and values, but those views would not be organized into opposing armies. Deliberation would replace debate. Collaboration would replace competition. The question would shift from "How do I win?" to "What policy actually makes sense?"

Evidence from citizens' assemblies around the world supports this prediction powerfully. Ireland's Citizens' Assembly, composed of randomly selected citizens, successfully tackled issues that had paralyzed elected politicians for decades — including abortion rights and same-sex marriage. These ordinary citizens, drawn from across Irish society, engaged in respectful deliberation, heard from experts, weighed competing values, and arrived at recommendations that the broader public endorsed through referenda. They did so without party whips, without attack ads, without cable news shouting matches. The French Citizens' Convention on Climate, composed of 150 randomly selected citizens, produced detailed and ambitious climate policy recommendations after months of deliberation. In both cases, the quality of discourse and the sophistication of outcomes exceeded what elected legislatures had produced.

The reason is straightforward: when people are not fighting for political survival, they can actually think. They can change their minds without being accused of betrayal. They can acknowledge the merits of opposing arguments without being primaried. They can prioritize problem-solving over messaging. Sortition creates the conditions for genuine deliberation — the kind of thoughtful, evidence-informed conversation that democracy was always supposed to enable but that elections systematically prevent.

IV. Empowering Ordinary People and Achieving True Representation

The current Congress is a grotesque distortion of the American population. Over half of its members are millionaires. The vast majority are lawyers, businesspeople, or career politicians. Women remain underrepresented relative to their share of the population. Racial minorities, working-class Americans, young people, and those without college degrees are dramatically underrepresented. The average age of a senator is over 64. Congress looks, thinks, and lives nothing like the country it governs.

This is not an accident. It is the inevitable result of a system where gaining power requires money, connections, ambition, and a willingness to endure the brutal gauntlet of modern campaigning. The electoral system selects for a very specific type of person — wealthy, well-connected, professionally ambitious, often narcissistic, and skilled at self-promotion. These traits may help someone win an election, but they have little correlation with the ability to govern wisely or to understand the lives of ordinary citizens.

Sortition produces a legislature that is a statistical mirror of the population. A body of 500 randomly selected American adults would, by the laws of probability, include roughly 250 women. It would include proportional numbers of Black, Latino, Asian, and Native Americans. It would include truck drivers, nurses, teachers, retail workers, and small business owners. It would include people who struggle to pay rent, people who lack health insurance, people who worry about the cost of childcare. For the first time in American history, the people making policy about healthcare would include significant numbers of people who have experienced the healthcare system as patients rather than as privileged consumers of premium care. The people making decisions about education funding would include teachers and parents rather than donors and lobbyists.

This descriptive representation matters enormously. Research in political science consistently shows that legislators' personal backgrounds influence their priorities and decisions. Women legislators are more likely to advance policies affecting women's health and family welfare. Legislators from working-class backgrounds are more attentive to labor issues. When the legislature looks like the country, the legislation is more likely to serve the country.

But sortition does more than change who governs — it changes how governance feels. In the current system, political power is something that belongs to others, to a professional class that ordinary citizens can petition but never join unless they possess extraordinary resources or ambition. Sortition transforms every citizen into a potential governor. The knowledge that you might be called to serve — that your neighbor, your coworker, your family member might be called to serve — fundamentally changes the relationship between citizen and state. It replaces alienation with ownership. It replaces the passive act of voting with the active possibility of governing.

Jury duty offers a useful analogy. Despite its inconveniences, jury service represents one of the last spaces in American public life where ordinary citizens exercise real governmental power. Studies consistently show that jury service increases civic engagement and trust in the justice system. Jurors report that the experience changes how they understand government and their role in it. Sortition for legislative and executive bodies would create this effect on a national scale, transforming millions of Americans from spectators into participants.

V. Addressing Objections: Competence, Manipulation, and Accountability

The most common objection to sortition is that ordinary citizens lack the competence to govern. This objection deserves a serious response, but it ultimately fails.

First, it relies on the demonstrably false assumption that elected officials are competent. The current Congress has repeatedly demonstrated an inability to address the nation's most pressing challenges — from climate change to healthcare to infrastructure to immigration. Members of Congress routinely display shocking ignorance about the subjects they regulate, as anyone who has watched a congressional hearing on technology can attest. The bar for competence is far lower than critics of sortition assume.

Second, the objection misunderstands how sortition would work in practice. No serious proposal for sortition suggests dropping randomly selected citizens into the existing congressional framework with no preparation or support. The most developed proposals include extensive onboarding periods, access to nonpartisan expert advisors, structured deliberative processes, and institutional support systems designed to help citizen-legislators engage with complex policy. The Irish and French citizens' assemblies demonstrated conclusively that ordinary people, given adequate time, information, and facilitative support, can engage with highly complex issues and produce sophisticated policy recommendations. The key insight is that competence is not a fixed trait — it is a product of institutional design. Create the right institutional conditions, and ordinary citizens govern extraordinarily well.

Third, the competence objection carries a deeply anti-democratic implication. If ordinary people cannot be trusted to govern, then democracy itself is illegitimate. The entire premise of democratic self-governance is that the people possess the collective wisdom to direct their own affairs. If we truly believe that only a specialized elite can govern, we should be honest about advocating for technocracy or aristocracy rather than hiding behind a democratic facade.

The concern about manipulation — that randomly selected citizens would be easy targets for sophisticated lobbyists and special interests — is also addressable through institutional design. Citizen-legislators could be insulated from lobbying through strict contact rules, provided with independent research staff, and required to engage with a balanced range of expert perspectives. Deliberative processes can be structured to expose manipulation and encourage critical thinking. Again, the evidence from citizens' assemblies is encouraging: ordinary citizens consistently demonstrate an impressive ability to evaluate competing claims, question expert witnesses, and reach independent judgments when given proper support.

The accountability objection — that randomly selected leaders cannot be voted out — requires a reconceptualization of accountability. Electoral accountability is largely mythological in practice. Incumbents win reelection at rates exceeding 90 percent in the House, regardless of performance. Gerrymandering ensures that most seats are safe for one party. Voters make decisions based on party loyalty, name recognition, and tribal identity far more than on evaluation of performance. The electoral model's accountability is largely theoretical.

Sortition offers different but real forms of accountability. Term limits are built into the system — citizens serve a single term and then return to live under the laws they created. This creates a powerful form of accountability that elected officials never face: the certainty that you will soon be a private citizen subject to your own decisions. Additionally, sortition bodies could be combined with mechanisms for citizen recall, judicial review, and public transparency requirements that provide meaningful oversight without the distorting incentives of electoral campaigns.

VI. A Practical Vision for Sortition in America

Implementing sortition in the United States would require careful, phased design, but it is far from impractical. A realistic model might proceed as follows:

The Legislature: Both chambers of Congress would be replaced by a single sortition body of 500 to 1,000 citizens, randomly selected from the eligible adult population using stratified sampling to ensure geographic and demographic representativeness. Members would serve staggered terms of two to three years, with a portion rotating out regularly to maintain institutional continuity. New members would undergo an intensive orientation period with nonpartisan educational support. Specialized committees would be supported by expert advisory panels, and all deliberations would be conducted using structured facilitation methods proven effective in citizens' assemblies worldwide.

The Executive: The head of government could be selected by the sortition legislature from among its own members or from a separate randomly selected pool, serving a fixed term with clearly defined powers. Alternatively, executive functions could be distributed among multiple citizen-leaders to prevent concentration of power.

The Judiciary: The existing judicial system could remain largely intact, providing constitutional review and legal oversight of the sortition bodies. This separation of powers would serve as a crucial check on potential abuses.

Civil Service: The permanent professional bureaucracy would continue to provide technical expertise, policy implementation, and institutional memory, ensuring that government functions continue smoothly regardless of turnover in the sortition bodies.

Transition: Implementation could begin at the local and state levels, building public familiarity and institutional expertise before scaling to the federal government. Pilot programs in cities and states would generate evidence, build public confidence, and allow for iterative improvement.

VII. The Moral Imperative

Ultimately, the case for sortition rests on a moral claim about human equality. Elections, by their nature, create a division between the governing and the governed, between those with the resources and temperament to compete for power and those who can only watch from the sidelines. This division is not merely procedural — it is a profound inequality that shapes every aspect of political life. It determines whose interests are represented, whose voices are heard, whose lives are valued by the machinery of government.

Sortition embodies the radical democratic promise that every citizen is equally capable of contributing to self-governance — that the truck driver's judgment is as valuable as the senator's, that the teacher's perspective matters as much as the lobbyist's, that the young single mother working two jobs has as much right to shape policy as the billionaire donor hosting a fundraiser.

The American experiment began with the revolutionary idea that ordinary people could govern themselves. Over two and a half centuries, that idea has been steadily betrayed by a system that concentrates power in the hands of a professional political class beholden to wealth and organized interests. The machinery of elections — the money, the media, the manipulation — has created a government that is democratic in name but oligarchic in practice.

Sortition offers a path back to the original promise. Not by returning to the past, but by moving forward to a system that takes democratic equality seriously — that trusts ordinary citizens not just to vote for their rulers but to become their own rulers. The technology, the institutional knowledge, and the evidence base all exist to make this transition possible. What remains is the political will to imagine a democracy worthy of the name.

The question before us is not whether sortition is perfect — no system of governance is. The question is whether it would be better than what we have. Given the depth of corruption, the intensity of partisanship, the crisis of legitimacy, and the systematic exclusion of ordinary citizens from meaningful political power, the answer is overwhelmingly clear.

It is time to trust the people — all of them, chosen by lot, empowered to govern. It is time for sortition.

  • Whether small-scale citizens' assembly success would translate to permanent national governance
  • How to handle executive functions requiring rapid, decisive action

  • How to ensure accountability when officials weren't chosen for their positions
  • Whether the public would accept the legitimacy of leaders chosen by lottery
  • Foreign policy and crisis management under collective amateur leadership
  • The role of genuine political skill and leadership in democratic governance

The sortition argument is ultimately a challenge to a deep assumption: that competitive selection of leaders through campaigns and voting is the best or only legitimate form of democratic governance.
