The Lottery of Liberty: A Call for Sortition in America

My fellow Americans,

Let me ask you a simple question — one that should trouble every citizen who still believes in the promise carved into the foundations of this republic:

When was the last time you felt truly represented?

Not pandered to. Not marketed to. Not spoken at during a campaign rally by a millionaire in a hard hat pretending to understand your life. When was the last time you looked at your government and said, "Those are my people. That is my voice."

I suspect, for most of you, the answer is... never.

And I'm here today to tell you that is not your failure. It is not apathy. It is not ignorance. It is the predictable, inevitable, structural consequence of a system that was broken before you were born — a system we call "elections" — and one we have been trained, since childhood, never to question.

Well, today, I am questioning it. And I am asking you to question it with me.

I. The Sacred Cow

We treat elections as though they were handed down on stone tablets. As though democracy and elections are synonyms. They are not. They never were.

The ancient Athenians — the very people who invented the word democracy — understood something we have forgotten. They used sortition: the random selection of citizens to hold public office. Not because they lacked the ability to hold elections. They held elections too — but they considered them aristocratic, a tool of the elite. Selection by lot, they believed, was the true mechanism of democracy.

Aristotle himself wrote it plainly: "The appointment of magistrates by lot is thought to be democratic, and the election of them oligarchic."

Let that sink in. The founders of democracy looked at elections and saw oligarchy — rule by the few, the powerful, the well-connected. And here we are, twenty-four centuries later, proving them right.

II. The Illusion of Choice

Let's be honest about what our elections actually produce.

Look at the United States Congress. The median net worth of a member of Congress is over one million dollars. In a nation where the median household struggles to cover a $400 emergency, our so-called "representatives" live in a different universe.

Over 90% of House races are won by the candidate who raises the most money. Ninety percent. That is not democracy. That is an auction.

And who funds these auctions? You know the answer. Corporations, PACs, billionaire donors, and industry lobbyists who expect — and receive — returns on their investment. A Princeton study by Gilens and Page examined twenty years of policy data and concluded what many of us already felt in our bones: the preferences of ordinary Americans have a near-zero statistical impact on public policy. Near zero. The preferences of economic elites and organized interest groups? Those move the needle.

You can vote every two years, every four years, in every primary and every general election — and the machinery doesn't flinch. It absorbs your vote like the ocean absorbs a raindrop, and the same class of people, beholden to the same class of donors, continues to legislate in their interest, not yours.

We don't have a democracy. We have a donor class with a PR department.

And elections are their stage.

III. The Corruption Engine

But the corruption isn't just about money — though the money is staggering. It's about what the electoral system selects for.

Think about what it takes to win an election in America today. You need name recognition. You need media connections. You need charisma — not wisdom, not empathy, not expertise — charisma. You need the stomach to spend 40, 50, 60 percent of your time in office fundraising for the next election. You need the willingness to make promises you cannot keep, to oversimplify problems you barely understand, and to demonize your opponents because fear and outrage drive turnout.

Elections do not select for the best among us. They select for the most ambitious, the most connected, and the most ruthless. They select for people who want power — and as history teaches us again and again, the people who want power the most are precisely the people who should have it the least.

The system is not broken. It is working exactly as designed — to filter out ordinary citizens and elevate a political class that serves itself.

IV. The Radical, Simple, Revolutionary Alternative

So here is my proposal. It is not new. It is not untested. It is as old as democracy itself.

Abolish elections for legislative and executive office. Replace them with sortition — the random selection of citizens to govern.

Here is how it works in its simplest form:

From the eligible adult population of the United States, we randomly select members of Congress — the House, the Senate, and yes, even the executive — the way we currently summon citizens for jury duty. Selected citizens would serve for a defined term — say, three years — with proper compensation, training, support staff, and access to expert testimony. They would deliberate, debate, and decide — and then they would return to their lives, making way for the next randomly chosen cohort.

No campaigns. No donors. No attack ads. No gerrymandering. No incumbency. No career politicians. No lobbyist lunches. No revolving door between Congress and K Street. No partisan primaries designed to elevate extremists. No multi-billion-dollar election industry feeding on division.

Just... citizens. Doing the work of self-governance. And going home.

V. "But Random People Can't Govern!"

I hear the objection already. It's the first one everyone raises, and I want to address it head-on, because it reveals a deep sickness in our political culture.

"Random people aren't qualified to make laws!"

My friends — look at who is making laws now.

We have members of Congress who don't understand how the internet works writing technology regulation. We have legislators who deny basic climate science overseeing environmental policy. We have representatives who have been in office for forty years and still can't pass a functioning budget.

The bar is not high.

But more importantly, the objection itself is an insult to the American people. It says, in effect: You cannot be trusted with your own governance. You are too ignorant, too unsophisticated, too ordinary to participate in democracy except by choosing between two pre-approved candidates every few years.

That is not a democratic belief. That is an aristocratic belief wearing democratic clothing.

The evidence tells a different story. Citizens' assemblies — randomly selected deliberative bodies — have been convened in Ireland, France, Canada, Australia, Belgium, and dozens of other places. They have tackled issues like abortion rights, climate policy, constitutional reform, and electoral systems. And the results, again and again, are remarkable.

In Ireland, a citizens' assembly of 99 randomly selected people recommended legalizing same-sex marriage and repealing the abortion ban — issues that the elected parliament had dodged for decades out of political cowardice. The people led. The politicians followed.

Why? Because they have no donors to please. No election to win. No base to perform for. They can simply... think.

Roughly half would be women. A proportionate number would be Black, Latino, Asian American, Indigenous. You would see nurses, truck drivers, teachers, cashiers, veterans, small business owners, retirees, and twenty-somethings still paying off student loans.

You would see the single mother who works two jobs and knows exactly what it means when Congress debates the minimum wage. You would see the farmer who doesn't need a lobbyist to explain agricultural policy because he lives it. You would see the veteran who doesn't need a think-tank white paper to understand the cost of war because she carries it in her body.

That is representation. Not the hollow, performative kind we have now — where a millionaire puts on a flannel shirt and eats a corn dog at the state fair. The real kind. The kind where the people who are affected by the laws are the same people who write them.

Random selection is the most statistically democratic method ever devised. It doesn't just give everyone an equal vote — it gives everyone an equal chance to govern. That is a depth of equality our current system cannot even dream of.

Let me be clear about something: sortition doesn't just reduce corruption. It annihilates the conditions that make corruption possible.

Corruption requires continuity — the same people in power long enough to be captured. Sortition eliminates that. Every few years, the entire body turns over. There is no incumbency to protect, no career to build, no war chest to fill.

Corruption requires campaigns — because campaigns require money, and money creates debt, and debt creates obedience. Sortition eliminates campaigns entirely. There is nothing to fund. There is no one to buy.

Corruption requires parties — hierarchical organizations that enforce discipline, punish dissent, and prioritize institutional power over public good. Under sortition, there are no parties. There are only citizens, unbound by party loyalty, free to deliberate on the merits.

Corruption requires the revolving door — the promise that if you legislate favorably, a cushy lobbying job awaits. But a randomly selected citizen who serves once and returns to private life has no door to revolve through.

Every mechanism of corruption that plagues our current system is structurally dependent on elections. Remove elections, and you don't just drain the swamp — you fill it in, pave it over, and build a park.

For generations, we have been told a story about democracy. The story says: Your role is to vote. Your role is to choose. And then your role is to sit down, shut up, and let the professionals handle it.

That story has made us passive. It has made us cynical. It has convinced us that government is something that happens to us, not something we do.

Imagine what that would mean for civic culture. Imagine a nation where every adult citizen knows that at any time, they could be called to serve. Not to fight. Not to sit on a jury for two weeks. But to govern. To sit in the halls of power and shape the future of their country.

Imagine how differently you would engage with the news, with your community, with the great questions of our time, if you knew that the responsibility might fall on your shoulders.

Sortition doesn't just change who governs. It changes what it means to be a citizen. It transforms governance from a spectator sport into a shared practice. It restores the original, radical promise of democracy — not that we get to choose our rulers, but that we rule ourselves.

"What about expertise?" Legislators already rely on expert staff, committee briefings, and testimony. Randomly selected citizens would do the same — and they would actually listen, because they have no pre-committed ideological brand to maintain. Moreover, nothing prevents the creation of advisory councils of subject-matter experts. What changes is who makes the final decision — and that should always be the people.

"What about accountability?" Elected officials are theoretically accountable through re-election. In practice, gerrymandering and incumbency advantage mean that over 95% of House members are re-elected regardless of performance. That is not accountability. That is a rubber stamp. Under sortition, accountability comes through transparency, term limits inherent in the system, and the knowledge that you will soon return to live under the very laws you helped write.

"What about the presidency?" This is where imaginations stretch — and should. Consider an executive council, randomly selected, rather than a single individual. The imperial presidency is itself a relic of monarchical thinking. A deliberative executive body, drawn from the citizenry, checked by a randomly selected legislature, would distribute power in a way that no single ego could capture. The cult of personality that has poisoned our politics would simply... evaporate.

"Isn't this just chaos?" No. It is structure without oligarchy. Sortition bodies operate with rules of procedure, professional facilitation, access to information, and clear mandates. The Irish Citizens' Assembly didn't descend into chaos. Neither did the French Citizens' Convention on Climate. Neither did the hundreds of other deliberative assemblies conducted around the world. Ordinary people, given a clear task and real responsibility, rise to the occasion. They always have.

X. The Courage to Imagine

I know what the political establishment will say about this idea. They will call it naïve. They will call it dangerous. They will call it un-American.

Of course they will. Because this idea threatens everything they have. Every advantage, every connection, every dollar, every lever of power they have spent their careers accumulating. They will defend elections the way monarchs defended the divine right of kings — with absolute conviction, right up until the moment the world changed beneath their feet.

But I am not speaking to them.

I am speaking to you. The teacher who has watched education funding get gutted by legislators who send their own kids to private schools. The nurse who worked through a pandemic while Congress debated whether you deserved hazard pay. The veteran who came home to a broken VA system. The young person drowning in student debt while billionaires get tax cuts. The parent working two jobs who still can't afford childcare.

I am speaking to every American who has ever looked at Washington and thought, "They don't see me. They don't hear me. They don't care about me."

You are right. They don't. And they won't. Not because they are evil — though some may be — but because the system that put them there was never designed to center you. It was designed to center them — the ambitious, the connected, the wealthy, the political class.

Sortition is not a reform. It is not a tweak. It is a revolution in the truest sense of the word — a turning of the wheel back to the people. It says that democracy is not a brand, not a slogan, not a bumper sticker. Democracy is the radical, beautiful, terrifying proposition that ordinary human beings can govern themselves.

XI. The Call

Two hundred and fifty years ago, a group of colonists looked at the most powerful empire on Earth and said: We can do better. We can govern ourselves.

That was considered insane. Dangerous. Naïve.

They did it anyway.

Today, I am asking you to summon that same courage. Not to overthrow a foreign king, but to overthrow an idea — the idea that elections are the only path to democracy, that professional politicians are the only people capable of governance, that your role as a citizen begins and ends in a voting booth.

It doesn't. Your role begins when you demand a seat at the table — not as a voter, not as a donor, not as a demographic in a campaign strategy — but as a citizen-governor of your own republic.

Abolish the auction. End the theater. Dismantle the machine that has turned self-governance into a spectacle and citizenship into spectatorship.

Give the people the government that was always supposed to be theirs.

Choose sortition. Choose real democracy. Choose the radical, democratic faith that your neighbor — that you — can be trusted with the future of this nation.

Not because you are perfect. But because you are sovereign.

Thank you.
